emergencies.name: Fracture / Broken Bone
questions: Is the person conscious, breathing, and able to respond to you?
Is the bone protruding or visible through the skin (open fracture)?
Is there severe, spurting, or uncontrolled bleeding around the injury?
Can the patient feel light touch and wiggle fingers or toes below the break point?
firstAidSteps: Do NOT attempt to straighten, push back, or realign any deformed bone or joint.
If open fracture with bleeding: Apply sterile pressure around the bone edges, not directly on exposed bone.
Immobilize the limb using rigid items (trekking poles, padded tree branches, rolled foam sleeping pad).
Secure the splint above AND below the suspected fracture using triangular bandages or torn fabric.
Leave fingertips or toes visible to regularly check blood circulation and pulse.
Apply an ice pack or snow wrapped in a cloth for 15-20 minutes to minimize severe swelling.
Keep the patient warm and dry using emergency space blanket to prevent traumatic shock.
Administer pain relief (Ibuprofen or Acetaminophen) if the patient is fully conscious and uninjured internally.
Do NOT allow the patient to bear weight or walk on a broken lower limb.
warningSigns: Extremity turns pale, blue, or ice cold to touch (loss of vascular circulation)
Rapid onset of complete numbness or pins-and-needles sensation distal to injury
Signs of systemic shock: pale clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, confusion, dizziness
Bone penetrating skin with active heavy bleeding
emergencies.evacuationNote: Activate Satellite SOS (Garmin inReach / Apple Emergency SOS / PLB). Note GPS coordinates. Signal rescuers with 3 sharp whistle blasts or mirror flashes every 60 seconds.

emergencies.name: Breathing Problem / Altitude Sickness
questions: Is the trekker at high altitude (> 2,500m / 8,000ft) and experiencing gurgling cough or confusion?
Is the person wheezing, choking on food/debris, or having a severe asthma attack?
Are their lips, tongue, or nail beds turning blue or grey (cyanosis)?
Can they speak in full sentences or only 1-2 words between gasps?
firstAidSteps: If high altitude sickness (HAPE/HACE): IMMEDIATELY begin descent to lower altitude (even 500m makes a life-saving difference).
Sit the patient upright in a comfortable 'tripod' position (leaning forward with hands on knees) — never lie them flat.
Loosen all tight clothing, backpack chest straps, and neck collars.
If known asthmatic: Assist with their prescribed bronchodilator rescue inhaler (2-4 puffs via spacer every 15 mins).
If available and trained: Administer bottled medical oxygen or place patient in Gamow hyperbaric bag.
Keep patient calm; instruct slow, steady pursed-lip breathing (inhale 2 seconds through nose, exhale 4 seconds through lips).
Protect from freezing wind and insulate the ground beneath them.
Do NOT force heavy physical exertion during severe shortness of breath.
warningSigns: Pink frothy sputum or wet gurgling sounds in the chest (High Altitude Pulmonary Edema)
Severe ataxia: walking like drunk, confusion, inability to touch nose (High Altitude Cerebral Edema)
Stridor (high-pitched inspiratory sound) or complete airway obstruction
Loss of consciousness or lethargy
emergencies.evacuationNote: Immediate priority evacuation. If altitude related, descending is the primary treatment. Use emergency beacon for helicopter rescue if unable to walk.

emergencies.name: Bleeding / Severe Wound
questions: Is the blood spurting under high pressure or flowing continuously and heavily?
Is there an object (knife, rock, wood branch) still embedded inside the wound?
Is the wound located on an arm/leg or on the torso/neck/head?
Is the patient feeling dizzy, cold, faint, or unusually thirsty?
firstAidSteps: Apply immediate direct, firm pressure over the wound using sterile gauze, clean bandana, or gloved palm.
Maintain firm continuous pressure for AT LEAST 10 full minutes without lifting the pad to check.
If bleeding is arterial (bright red spurting) on an arm or leg and direct pressure fails: Apply a commercial or improvised TOURNIQUET 5-7cm (2-3 in) above wound, never over a joint.
Tighten tourniquet windlass until the bleeding stops completely; write the EXACT application time on patient's forehead (e.g., 'TK 14:35').
If an object is impaled: Do NOT remove it. Stabilize the object in place using bulky rolled dressings on both sides.
If direct pressure controls bleeding: Wrap firmly with an elastic pressure bandage.
Lay the patient down and elevate legs slightly if signs of shock develop (unless head/spine trauma).
Wrap patient in thermal space blanket to keep body core warm.
warningSigns: Tourniquet remains loose or blood continues heavy spurting
Rapid drop in consciousness, gray skin, shivering, rapid thready pulse
Wound is pulsating or located on junctional areas (groin, armpit, neck)
Massive blood loss exceeding 500ml
emergencies.evacuationNote: CRITICAL EMERGENCY. Evacuate urgently. Never loosen or remove a tourniquet once applied in the wilderness; only medical professionals should remove it.

emergencies.name: Hypothermia / Frostbite
questions: Is the trekker violently shivering, or have they STOPPED shivering while remaining lethargic and confused?
Are their clothes wet from rain, river crossing, or heavy sweat?
Are any fingers, toes, nose, or ears white, waxy, hard, or devoid of feeling (frostbite)?
Are they slurring words, fumbling gear (the 'umbles': mumbles, stumbles, fumbles)?
firstAidSteps: Move the person immediately out of wind and precipitation into a tent, bivy sack, or rock shelter.
Carefully strip off all wet clothing and replace with warm, dry synthetic/wool layers.
Create a 'Hypothermia Wrap': Lay insulated sleeping pads on ground, place patient inside sleeping bag, wrap exterior with waterproof tarp or space blanket.
Place gentle heat sources (warm water bottles wrapped in socks) on the chest, groin, and armpits — NEVER apply direct scalding heat.
If fully conscious and swallowing: Offer warm, sugary fluids (hot tea, soup, electrolyte broth). NEVER give alcohol or caffeine.
Handle the patient extremely gently — rough movements can trigger fatal cardiac ventricular fibrillation in severe hypothermia.
For frostbite: Do NOT rub with snow or massage frozen tissue. Do NOT thaw if there is ANY danger of refreezing before reaching hospital.
warningSigns: Shivering stops while body remains cold (indicates moderate-to-severe hypothermia < 32°C / 90°F)
Paradoxical undressing (patient takes off clothes despite freezing cold)
Severe bradycardia (pulse < 40 bpm) or unresponsiveness
Black, blistered, or wooden frozen tissue
emergencies.evacuationNote: Urgent passive and active rewarming during shelter. Request urgent wilderness rescue for severe hypothermia or deep frostbite.

emergencies.name: Snake / Insect / Venomous Bite
questions: Can you see 2 distinct puncture fang marks, rapid swelling, or bruising around the bite site?
Is the person experiencing difficulty breathing, throat swelling, hives, or dizziness (anaphylactic allergic shock)?
When did the bite occur (how many minutes ago)?
Can you describe the creature's shape, pattern, or head from a safe distance?
firstAidSteps: Move patient to a safe location away from the animal. Do NOT attempt to capture or kill the snake.
Keep the bitten person completely calm and STILL — physical movement speeds venom dissemination.
Position the bitten limb below the level of the heart.
Immediately remove all rings, watches, tight bracelets, and tight boots before swelling sets in.
Wash the bite gently with clean water and soap if available.
Apply a broad, firm pressure immobilization bandage (for neurotoxic/elapid bites) starting at fingers/toes moving upwards, snug like an ankle sprain.
Splint the limb to prevent joint flexing.
If severe allergic anaphylaxis: Administer Epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) into outer mid-thigh immediately.
NEVER cut the wound, NEVER suck venom, NEVER apply ice, and NEVER apply an arterial tourniquet for snakebites.
warningSigns: Difficulty swallowing, drooling, or eyelid drooping (ptosis)
Stridor, wheezing, tongue swelling, or systemic hives (anaphylaxis)
Bleeding from gums, old puncture sites, or blood in urine
Paralysis, muscle fasciculations, or seizures
emergencies.evacuationNote: Carry the patient on a stretcher/litter if possible to prevent walking. Mark leading edge of swelling on skin with pen and timestamp every 15 minutes.

emergencies.name: Cardiac Emergency / Chest Pain
questions: Is the person experiencing crushing chest pressure radiating to left arm, jaw, back, or neck?
Is the person conscious, responsive, and breathing normally?
Does the person have a known history of heart disease, angina, or prescribed Nitroglycerin?
Are they sweating profusely, nauseous, or struggling for breath?
firstAidSteps: Have the patient stop all physical movement immediately and sit in a comfortable semi-reclined 'W-position' with knees bent.
If conscious and non-allergic: Have the patient chew one full adult Aspirin (300-325mg) or four low-dose baby Aspirins (81mg each).
If patient has prescribed Nitroglycerin and systolic BP is adequate: Assist with one sublingual spray/tablet under the tongue.
Loosen collar, belt, and pack harness.
Reassure the patient continuously to lower adrenaline and myocardial oxygen demand.
IF PATIENT BECOMES UNRESPONSIVE AND NOT BREATHING: Immediately start CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation).
CPR Protocol: 100-120 chest compressions per minute in center of chest, 5-6 cm deep. 30 compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths (or continuous Hands-Only CPR).
warningSigns: Sudden collapse and loss of consciousness
Absence of carotid pulse or agonal gasping breaths
Gray cyanotic skin with cold diaphoresis (sweating)
Chest pain worsening despite rest and aspirin
emergencies.evacuationNote: CRITICAL LIFE THREAT. Trigger instant SOS. If cardiac arrest occurs, continue CPR without interruption while calling for helicopter medevac.

emergencies.name: Head Injury / Concussion
questions: Did the person lose consciousness, even for a few seconds?
Is there clear or blood-tinged fluid draining from their ears or nose?
Is the person repeating questions, confused about time/location, or experiencing severe projectile vomiting?
Was there high-energy trauma (fall from height, rock impact) indicating possible spinal neck injury?
firstAidSteps: If fall or neck pain suspected: Manually stabilize the cervical spine (hold head in neutral alignment, do NOT twist neck).
Check level of consciousness using AVPU scale (Alert, Voice responsive, Pain responsive, Unresponsive).
If scalp is bleeding: Apply gentle direct pressure with clean gauze (avoid pushing down hard if skull fracture is felt).
Keep the person lying still, resting quietly in a shaded, calm area.
Do NOT give sedatives, sleeping pills, or aspirin (use Acetaminophen for mild headache only).
Monitor pupil size, symmetry, and responsiveness to light.
Wake the patient every 2 hours through the night to check orientation and speech coherence.
Do not allow the patient to return to trekking, climbing, or carrying a backpack.
warningSigns: Unequal pupil sizes or eyes not tracking together
Repeated persistent vomiting (> 2 episodes)
Worsening confusion, slurred speech, or progressive drowsiness
Bruising behind the ears (Battle's sign) or black eyes ('raccoon eyes')
emergencies.evacuationNote: Any loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, or spinal pain requires immediate evacuation on a backboard/litter.

emergencies.name: Heat Stroke / Severe Exhaustion
questions: Is the patient's skin hot and dry with an ABSENCE of sweat, and are they confused or delirious (Heat Stroke)?
Is the trekker experiencing intense muscle cramps, nausea, headache, and weakness (Heat Exhaustion)?
Can the patient keep fluids down without vomiting?
How long have they been exposed to direct sun and high heat?
firstAidSteps: Move the person immediately into dense shade or pitch a tarp for shelter.
For suspected HEAT STROKE (Emergency): Aggressively cool immediately — soak clothing in cold stream water and fan vigorously.
Apply wet bandanas or ice packs to high-flow vascular zones: neck, armpits, and groin.
Elevate legs 20-30 cm if heat exhaustion faintness occurs.
If conscious and not vomiting: Administer small, frequent sips of cool water with oral rehydration salts (ORS) or electrolyte mix.
Do NOT give salt tablets directly without water.
Remove unnecessary outer layers, pack gear, and heavy boots.
Rest until core temperature normalizes and symptoms resolve completely.
warningSigns: Altered mental state: delirium, hallucinations, aggressive behavior, seizures
Hot flushed skin that has stopped sweating
Rapid bounding pulse followed by weak thready pulse
Inability to stand or severe collapse
emergencies.evacuationNote: Heat stroke is an acute medical emergency with high mortality. Rapid aggressive cooling on-site is mandatory while arranging medevac.
